What if BMW's New i3 Is Right and Everything We Know About Designing a Modern Sedan Is Wrong?
9 photos
Photo: WheelsAge
There's something slightly awkward about the all-new BMW i3. It obviously has everything to do with its Neue Klasse design language, which to be fair does come with a suitably futuristic-looking front end, clean bumper-to-bumper surfaces, and a properly futuristic rear end.
Yet, whenever I look at it from the side, or even a front 3/4 angle, the proportions seem a little off. The hood is too short, the passenger compartment sits too far forward (also known as a cab-forward aesthetic), and it's almost like there's not enough room between the front doors and the front wheels.
I reckon much of that awkwardness comes down to what we're accustomed to seeing on a regular basis. For the better part of a century, the traditional sedan has adhered to a fairly predictable formula. It's got a relatively long hood, either a mid-cab or a cab-rearward aesthetic, and a trunk extending well beyond the rear window. Of course, we've seen a whole bunch of variations, but the basic proportions have remained consistent.
BMW spent decades perfecting this formula so that it may reflect favorably upon their products. From the E39 5er to the E46 3 Series, or even the outgoing G20 and G30 - they all have a long hood, a short front overhang and a rearward positioning of the cabin. The latter has always been fundamental to the brand's design identity , and we associate these proportions with sportiness. We don't even need to see a badge. Even a silhouette would suffice.
To me, a BMW sedan is supposed to look like a rear-wheel drive car, and I'm sure I'm not the only one who feels that way.
But there's a flip side to that argument. Throughout history, the engineers were more or less in charge of these specific proportions, as opposed to the designers. You need room at the front for a longitudinally mounted engine, especially of the six or eight-cylinder variety. Then you add the transmission, cooling, crash structures... and you eventually land on a substantial front end with a long hood.
Photo: WheelsAge Over time, these necessities became synonymous with performance and even elegance. Whereas a short hood, well, that's something you'd expect to find on a compact budget car or a minivan - something that's trying to maximize interior space so as to make up for everything else it's lacking (usually quality and/or performance).
This is why I'm singling out the new i3 . What BMW have done is that they've messed around with one of the most recognizable silhouettes in the industry. Gone are your traditional BMW sedan proportions and here comes this cab-forward experiment, with a less dominant hood and a more dominant cabin. The ratio between the front axle and the windshield is quite different than what we've come to expect from any 3 Series derivative. It'll take some getting used to, that's for sure.
But here's the thing. More recently, I've been wondering whether this reaction says more about the car itself or about the way we've been conditioned to perceive car design in general? An electric motor occupies a fraction of the space required by a combustion engine, and there's no inherent reason for the cabin to sit as far back as it traditionally sits. By moving it forward, you free up space for the occupants, and you can improve the overall package efficiency. I get all that.
And still, this is 100% a choice. Make no mistake about it. Look at the Model S , the OG EV, so to speak. Tesla could have designed it any which way, but they chose to go with a conventional premium "sedan" shape. I say "sedan" because it's technically a fastback, but the point is that it's got a long hood - like you'd expect from a combustion engine car.
Wait, haven't we seen this before? If you mean the cab-forward aesthetic, yes. Yes we have. Allow me to take you back to the 90s and to Chrysler's LH-platform sedans, the Dodge Intrepid and the Chrysler Concorde. Both these cars had their windshields pushed forward, relatively short hoods, and barely any distance between the front doors and the wheel wells. Almost no distance, actually.
Photo: WheelsAge They looked properly futuristic compared to all those boxy sedans that preceded them. Yet cab-forward design never became the universal standard. I guess people just weren't ready for it.
But now imagine someone born in 2040 (and getting their driver's license in 2058) looking back at a BMW 3 Series from 2020. The idea of dedicating such a large proportion of a sedan's overall length to the engine compartment could look peculiar to that person if future vehicles go on to abandon the long-hood aesthetic altogether.
Would that person even find the G20 elegant or good-looking? Would a long hood still communicate sportiness to us? It's an interesting thought experiment. There's no guarantee that our current understanding of what makes a sedan beautiful will endure another 50-100 years. Besides, I already told you where I think the three-box sedan is going in the long term - extinct. I think fastbacks are going to take over eventually. But that's hardly the point of this op-ed.
The point is that maybe myself, and others like me, we just don't "get" the new i3. We don't perceive it the way it's meant to be perceived. I'm willing to give it the benefit of the doubt. I still think the G50 3 Series looks better, but I can certainly change my opinion if the i3 somehow wins me over. I look forward to reviewing it for you guys as soon as possible.
I also realize that I've spent my entire life looking at cars with proportions shaped by the need to accommodate combustion engines. Maybe this is the part worth questioning. It's entirely plausible (not probable) that 20 years from now, we might look back at the second-generation i3 and see an early example of BMW establishing a new norm in terms of three-box sedan proportions.
